drills.q: Why does cross-lingual retrieval work with zero shared vocabulary between query and document?
drills.a: The embedding model was trained with a contrastive objective on cross-lingual pairs known/inferred to share meaning, pulling translation-equivalent text together in vector space regardless of shared tokens -- the training signal only ever optimized for shared meaning, not shared language.

drills.q: What is tokenizer fertility and give its rough cost multiplier for non-English languages.
drills.a: Tokens produced per word/character. Non-English, especially morphologically rich or non-Latin-script languages, often pay 1.5-2x+ the per-character token cost of English -- a direct compute/latency/context-budget tax.

drills.q: A 22-locale product's blended recall@k dashboard looks healthy but one locale is quietly broken. Explain the mechanism and the fix.
drills.a: A blended metric averages across all locales, so one language collapsing to near-zero is mathematically absorbed by the other 21 healthy languages. Fix: report and alert on recall@k/nDCG per locale as a hard requirement, never rely on a single blended number.

drills.q: Compare the operational cost of a shared multilingual index versus per-language indexes.
drills.a: Shared index is simplest to operate (one index, one model, one monitoring surface) but risks cross-lingual leakage hidden by blended metrics. Per-language indexes isolate quality and allow language-specific models but multiply build/monitor/reindex work by locale count -- a real cost at 22 locales, not a rounding error.

drills.q: Why does a whitespace-based lexical tokenizer break on CJK text, and what's the fix?
drills.a: CJK scripts have no whitespace between words, so a whitespace tokenizer either treats every character as its own token (destroying word-level meaning BM25 needs) or fails to segment. Fix: dedicated segmenters like Jieba (Chinese) or MeCab (Japanese) before lexical indexing.

drills.q: A user types a romanized query for a language natively written in a non-Latin script and gets zero results. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: The index holds only native-script content and the romanized query shares no tokens or embedding-space proximity with it. Fix by normalizing via transliteration at index time, at query time, or choosing/fine-tuning a model with demonstrated transliteration robustness -- romanized input is common, not a rare edge case.

drills.q: How should a language detector handle a code-switched query like "what's the estado del clima today"?
drills.a: Single top-1 detection forces an artificial single-language label on inherently mixed content. Use top-k predictions; when top-2 are close in confidence, run retrieval across both candidate languages and fuse, or fall back to the shared multilingual embedding space, which doesn't need a language label at all.

drills.q: Why might a model advertised as supporting "100+ languages" still underperform for several of your active locales?
drills.a: Aggregate language-count claims say nothing about per-language training data volume. Low-resource languages sit in the weaker tail by construction. Validate per-locale against your own golden set rather than trusting the vendor's headline benchmark.

drills.q: Design the per-locale evaluation and monitoring strategy for a 22-locale RAG product going into production.
drills.a: Build a golden set stratified by language, ideally native-speaker-annotated (not machine-translated from an English set). Report recall@k/nDCG per locale as a first-class metric with independent alerting thresholds. Track tokenizer fertility/cost per locale separately. Route language detection with a confidence threshold and shared-embedding fallback for ambiguous queries. Re-run the full per-locale eval on every embedding model swap or reindex.

drills.q: When would translate-then-retrieve still be the right call in 2026 despite multilingual embeddings being the modern default?
drills.a: For a genuinely low-resource language where the multilingual embedding's alignment is weak from insufficient training data -- translating the query into a high-resource pivot language, retrieving there, and translating results back can outperform a poorly-aligned multilingual embedding, since the translation model may have stronger signal for that language pair.
